crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Judicial Analytics
children.blurb: Judicial analytics is the study of courts, judges, and litigation outcomes using data and computational methods.

children.name: Opposing Counsel and Docket Patterns
children.blurb: Opposing counsel and docket patterns is the study of how lawyers and courts behave across the life of a case, using public filings to see what each side tends to file, when, and with what result.

children.name: Settlement Valuation and Risk
children.blurb: Settlement valuation and risk is the practice of estimating the likely financial terms of a civil settlement and the probability of various outcomes if a dispute proceeds to trial or arbitration.

children.name: Jury Selection and Public Data
children.blurb: Jury selection and public data covers the use of openly available information about prospective jurors to inform the exercise of peremptory challenges and cause challenges during voir dire.

children.name: Live Testimony Cross-Referencing
children.blurb: Live testimony cross-referencing covers the real-time comparison of a witness's spoken answers in a hearing, deposition, or trial with the existing record.

sections.body: Litigation prediction and judicial analytics is the use of AI to read court records, briefs, rulings, dockets, jury data, and transcripts to estimate how cases, judges, opposing counsel, and juries may behave. In practice, systems extract patterns from past decisions, track motion outcomes, compare counsel histories, and score settlement ranges. They do not replace legal judgment. They help lawyers prepare, spot inconsistencies, and test arguments. The work is mostly statistical and text based, not a crystal ball. It draws on public and commercial datasets, with limits on coverage and quality.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts are more mature, while others remain experimental. Docket analytics and judge histories are widely used because records are structured enough, but settlement valuation models depend on assumptions and jurisdiction. Jury selection tools often rely on public data that may be sparse or biased, and live testimony cross referencing is emerging, useful for flagging contradictions but not for deciding credibility. The honest limits include opaque models, incomplete records, sealed documents, and the risk of encoding past bias. No model can predict a specific ruling or verdict with certainty. The site tracks 149 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, and 29 AI case law precedents, which shows how fast the underlying law is still moving.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages under this section fit together as a workflow. Judicial Analytics covers how judges' past rulings and writing styles are modeled. Opposing Counsel and Docket Patterns looks at the other side's filing habits and procedural timing. Settlement Valuation and Risk turns those signals into ranges and risk factors. Jury Selection and Public Data examines what can and cannot be inferred from public records about jurors, while Live Testimony Cross-Referencing focuses on real time or post hoc comparison of statements against transcripts and evidence. A reader would go to each for a different layer of preparation, from judge to opponent to money to jury to testimony.
